Nothing at all, because switches encrypt frames
Only frames whose source MAC matches your OUI
explain: Promiscuous mode makes your card accept every frame it receives, but the switch only sends your port the frames meant for you plus broadcasts and multicasts. Seeing other hosts' traffic needs a hub, a mirror port on the switch (a port configured to receive copies of other ports' traffic), or tricking the switch or the hosts, which is exactly what layer 2 attacks try.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: TCP: handshake, sequence numbers, flags and teardown
question: The client's ISN is 7000. It sends SYN, completes the handshake, then sends 250 bytes. What acknowledgment number should the server send after receiving them?
explain: The SYN consumes sequence number 7000, so data starts at 7001. 250 bytes cover 7001 to 7250, and the acknowledgment names the next expected byte: 7251.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: HTTPS and TLS at a glance: what encryption hides and what it does not
question: A user connects to `https://bank.example`. Why can a device in the middle (say, after ARP spoofing) not simply read the traffic by pretending to be the bank?
options: Because ARP spoofing does not work on Wi-Fi
Because the device cannot present a certificate for bank.example signed by an authority the browser trusts, so the handshake fails or warns
Because TLS hides the IP addresses
Because port 443 cannot be intercepted
explain: The device can relay packets, but to decrypt it must complete the TLS handshake as bank.example, and that requires a trusted certificate and the matching private key. Without them the browser shows an error. The attack then depends on the user ignoring the warning.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Memory policies: local, bind, preferred and interleave
question: A service is started with `numactl --membind=0` on a 2-node box. Node 0 has 64 GiB, node 1 has 64 GiB, and the service grows to 80 GiB. What happens?
options: The extra 16 GiB is allocated on node 1 automatically
The kernel switches the process to interleave mode
Allocations that node 0 cannot satisfy fail, because bind never falls back to node 1
explain: MPOL_BIND restricts allocation to the listed nodes. numactl(8) says allocation will fail when there is not enough memory on them. If spilling to node 1 is acceptable, use --preferred=0 instead.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Why flash cannot overwrite a page in place
question: A drive uses a direct-mapped layout with 256 KB erase blocks of 4 KB pages. The host overwrites a single 4 KB page. How many page programs does the flash perform?
options: 1, because only one page changed
63, the other live pages
64, the whole block is rewritten after the erase
128, one read and one program per page
explain: After erasing, every page of the block is blank, so all 64 pages (63 preserved plus the new one) must be programmed. That is 64x more flash writing than the host asked for, and the block takes one more P/E cycle per host write.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Parallel flash and the NVMe queue interface
question: A host driver reaps completions by checking the phase tag. After the CQ wraps from the last slot back to slot 0, what must the driver do?
options: Nothing: new entries always have phase tag 1
Reset every phase tag in the queue to 0
Read the controller's CQ tail register
Flip the phase value it expects, because the controller now writes the opposite bit
explain: On each wrap the controller inverts the phase tag it writes. The host tracks the expected value and flips it when its head wraps. The CQ tail is internal to the controller and not visible to the host.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Training and tuning a detector in practice
question: You call `model.predict(img, conf=0.25, iou=0.7)` and see two boxes on one car with IoU 0.6 between them. Which change removes the duplicate?
options: Set iou=0.5 so NMS suppresses boxes overlapping by more than 0.5
Raise conf to 0.5
Set iou=0.9
Set max_det=1
explain: Here `iou` is the NMS threshold: boxes overlapping a higher-scoring box by more than it are removed. At 0.7 a 0.6 overlap survives; at 0.5 it is suppressed. Raising conf might drop the duplicate only if its score is low, and max_det=1 would discard every other car too.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Keeping object storage off the hot read path
question: In Neon, why does a COMMIT not include the latency of an object storage PUT?
options: Postgres batches commits for up to a second
Durability comes from a majority of safekeepers storing the WAL; pages reach object storage later, off the commit path
The compute node's local NVMe is replicated
Object storage writes are done with S3 Express One Zone
explain: Neon defines commit as WAL acknowledged by a quorum of safekeepers. The pageserver materializes pages and uploads them to object storage asynchronously. If a safekeeper dies, the quorum continues; if the pageserver dies, its state is rebuilt from WAL and object storage.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away
question: Which setup guarantees a complete trace for every request that returned a 500?
options: Tail sampling in the collector, which buffers a trace's spans and decides once they are complete
Head sampling at 1 in 10 plus a longer retention period
A trace-id ratio sampler at 0.01, since its decision is deterministic
Setting the sampled bit at the gateway only when the gateway sees an error
explain: Only a decision made after the spans exist can condition on the error. Longer retention keeps dropped spans dropped. A deterministic ratio sampler is still a ratio. The last option fails because the gateway must inject traceparent before the request runs, so at decision time the error has not happened yet, and the downstream spans would already have been dropped.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Scoring OCR output: edit distance, CER and WER
question: You must pick one metric to decide whether an invoice-total extractor is good enough for automatic payment. Which is most appropriate?
options: Average CER over all page text
Average WER over all page text
Exact match of the normalized total field per document
Detection F-score of text boxes
explain: Payment needs the exact amount. Page-level CER can look excellent while the one field that matters has a wrong digit. Field-level exact match after agreed normalization measures what the business cares about.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
question: Ana runs `chmod 777 /home/ana/notes.txt`. The SELinux policy does not allow the web server's domain to read files in home directories. Can a compromised web server read the file?
options: Yes, because DAC is checked last and wins
No, because the MAC check runs after DAC and refuses
No, because chmod 777 removes read permission
Yes, because 777 lets everyone read
explain: Both checks must say yes. DAC passes (others have r), then the LSM hook asks the mandatory policy, which the file's owner cannot override, and it refuses.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Dropping privileges correctly, and sudo's Baron Samedit
question: Why must setresgid come before setresuid when dropping from root?
options: It does not matter
setresuid resets the groups automatically
Group IDs are checked first by the kernel
After the UIDs leave 0 the process loses the capability needed to change GIDs, so a later setresgid would fail and leave root's group in place
explain: Changing GIDs and supplementary groups needs CAP_SETGID. Dropping the UIDs first clears the capabilities, so the group change fails, and if the return value is not checked the process keeps group 0.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: chroot is not a boundary, and Leaky Vessels shows why
question: Which of runc 1.1.12's fixes also protects against file descriptor leaks nobody has found yet?
options: Renaming /sys/fs/cgroup
Closing all internal descriptors before execve and checking that the working directory is inside the container
Marking the one known cgroup descriptor O_CLOEXEC
Disabling WORKDIR in Dockerfiles
explain: Fixing the known leak removes one hole. Closing every non-stdio descriptor and verifying the working directory with getcwd stop the whole class, which is why the advisory recommends them to other runtimes.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: What goes wrong: the confused deputy and TOCTOU races
question: Which change removes the TOCTOU window in a setuid program that calls access() then open()?
options: Dropping the separate check and opening the file with the caller's own effective UID (and O_NOFOLLOW)
Adding sleep() between the calls
Calling access() twice
Checking that the path string does not contain /etc
explain: Any separate check leaves a gap. Making the open itself run with the caller's identity lets the kernel do the check atomically on the file actually opened.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Ethics and law first: public is not the same as permitted
question: In the 2013 Reddit case, which missing control would have prevented the harm most directly?
options: A faster website
Using more photos
Better image resolution
Not publishing identifications without a mandate, expert verification and review
explain: The harm came from naming people on unverified guesses. More or sharper photos would have produced more confident wrong guesses; the fix is process: mandate, verification by qualified people, review before publication.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Mapping your own organisation's public footprint
question: Why is RDAP easier to automate than the old WHOIS?
options: It requires no internet connection
It shows registrants' home addresses
Queries are HTTPS addresses and replies are structured JSON
It only works for .com domains
explain: RFC 9082 defines queries as HTTP URLs and RFC 9083 defines JSON responses, so a script can parse fields reliably. Personal data is usually redacted, and RDAP serves many top-level domains (TLDs, such as .com or .org).

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Chronolocation: telling the time from shadows
question: A 2 m sign casts a 2 m shadow. What is the sun's elevation?
options: 90 degrees
30 degrees
45 degrees
60 degrees
explain: s/h = 1 means tan(elevation) = 1, so elevation is 45 degrees. Higher sun would give a shorter shadow; 30 degrees would give a ratio of about 1.73.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: People-search sites, data brokers and protecting your own footprint
question: What does the Pwned Passwords service learn when you check a password with the range API?
options: The full password
The full SHA-1 hash
Only a 5-character hash prefix shared by many passwords
Your email address
explain: Only the prefix is sent; matching happens locally, and padding hides the response size. That is the k-anonymity design.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
question: Library `img` uses libpng only inside img.cpp; its public header img.h never mentions png types. Which line is right?
options: target_link_libraries(img PUBLIC PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img INTERFACE PNG::PNG)
target_link_libraries(img PRIVATE PNG::PNG)
include_directories(/usr/include/libpng) at the top level
explain: Only the implementation uses libpng, so PRIVATE. PUBLIC would leak png's include paths and definitions to every consumer; INTERFACE would not give them to img.cpp itself, so img would fail to compile. A global include_directories bypasses targets entirely.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Jobs, needs and matrices: how one push becomes many runs
question: Your PR shows `test (windows-latest)` failed and `test (ubuntu-latest)` and `test (macos-latest)` cancelled. What do you know about Linux and macOS?
options: They passed, because only Windows is marked as failed
They also failed, because cancelled means failed
Nothing yet: with the default fail-fast, GitHub cancelled them when Windows failed
They were skipped because they need the Windows job
explain: `strategy.fail-fast` defaults to true and cancels in-progress and queued matrix jobs when any one fails. Cancelled jobs did not finish, so they give no information. Fix the Windows failure or set `fail-fast: false` to see all results.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
question: Which situation lets a reviewer withhold approval even if the code is clean and well tested?
options: The reviewer would have used a different but equally valid algorithm
The author used tabs where the style guide is silent and the file already uses tabs
The PR adds a feature the project has decided it does not want
The PR is 40 lines and the reviewer expected 30
explain: Google's guide explicitly allows denying a feature the maintainers do not want in their system, however well designed. An equally valid alternative should defer to the author, consistency with the existing file is correct, and line counts alone are not a reason.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Why reviewer response time dominates time to merge
question: A reviewer in another time zone sees that only two typo fixes remain. The author will be asleep for the next 10 hours. What does Google's guide suggest?
options: Request changes so the author fixes the typos, then review again tomorrow
Wait to approve until the typos are fixed, to keep the process strict
Approve with comments (LGTM with comments), noting the typos to fix before merging
Fix the typos and approve your own commit
explain: Minor remaining comments are exactly the case for LGTM with comments, and the guide calls it especially worth considering across time zones. Requesting another round costs the author a full extra day for two typos.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: Which action breaks the Linux kernel's guidance for AI coding assistants?
options: Adding an Assisted-by tag
Letting the assistant add a Signed-off-by line to the commit
Writing a reproducer before sending a bug fix
Stating in the changelog which tool found the bug
explain: Only humans can legally certify the DCO, so AI agents must not add Signed-off-by. The human submitter reviews the code, adds their own sign-off and takes responsibility. The other three are things the guidance asks for.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
question: Why does a plain `git push` fail right after a successful `git rebase upstream/main` on a branch you had already pushed?
options: The pushed commits were rewritten, so the remote tip is no longer an ancestor of your local tip
Rebase deletes the remote branch
GitHub blocks pushes to branches that have an open PR
Rebase changes the remote URL of origin
explain: Without force, git push only accepts fast-forward updates. Rebasing replaced your commits with new ones, so the old remote tip is no longer in your branch's history. Pushing to a branch with an open PR is normal and updates the PR.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: License compatibility: can these two pieces of code be combined?
question: Which pair can be combined into one distributed program?
options: GPL-2.0-only code inside a GPL-3.0-only project
MIT code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
GPL-3.0 code inside an Apache-2.0 project that stays Apache-2.0
Apache-2.0 code inside a GPL-2.0-only project
explain: MIT is GPL-compatible: its only condition is keeping the notice, which any GPL version allows. The other three either mix incompatible GPL versions, need the whole to become GPL, or add restrictions GPLv2 forbids.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Noise and bias: making before and after comparable
question: Why does benchstat's documentation recommend interleaving before and after runs?
options: It makes each individual run faster
Go benchmarks crash when run in blocks
So that slow changes in the machine (heat, background jobs) hit both versions evenly instead of only one
Because the U test requires alternating samples
explain: Noise must be spread evenly across both versions. In blocked order, any drift during the session is attributed entirely to whichever version ran later.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: git blame: who last changed a line, and seeing past noise
question: Plain git blame says every line of a function was last changed by a commit titled "Run formatter". What is the most useful next command?
options: `git log -1` on that commit and conclude its author wrote the function
`git blame --reverse file`
`git grep -p` on the function name
`git blame -w --ignore-rev <formatter-hash> file` to look past the formatting commit
explain: A formatting commit is the last modifier but not the author of the logic. Ignoring whitespace and the formatter commit points each line at the commit that changed its content. --reverse answers a different question: the last revision in which a line still existed.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Delta debugging: let a script shrink the repro
question: You give a reducer an interestingness test that returns success whenever the compiler exits with a non-zero code. The output is a tiny file that triggers a syntax error. What went wrong?
options: The reducer has a bug; delta debugging should never produce invalid input
The input was too large for delta debugging to handle
The test should have returned non-zero for interesting candidates
The test was not specific: a syntax error is also a non-zero exit, so the reducer drifted to a different, trivial failure
explain: Reducers keep whatever the test calls interesting. "Any non-zero exit" includes syntax errors, which are trivially easy to keep, so reduction slides toward them. Grep for the exact crash message or assertion so only the original bug counts.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: One logical change per PR, and every commit builds
question: A 5-commit series has commit 3 that does not compile (it was fixed in commit 4). Why might a maintainer ask you to fix this before merging with a merge commit?
options: Because git bisect may land on commit 3 and be unable to test it, hiding which commit introduced a later bug
Because CI only tests the first commit
Because GitHub refuses to merge a PR with a broken commit
Because commit 3 doubles the review time
explain: A merge commit keeps every commit on the main branch. Bisect can check out any of them; an untestable commit must be skipped, and if it is next to the culprit, git cannot say which one is first bad.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Inside the PagedAttention kernel
question: Why did vLLM's original key cache split each key into x-number chunks, with shape [..., head_size/x, block_size, x]?
options: To quantize keys to 8 bits
Because the head size must be a multiple of the block size
So the reduce kernel can merge partitions without shared memory
So a warp, with one thread group per token, reads the same 16-byte chunk of all 16 tokens in a block as one contiguous 256-byte run
explain: x = 16 / element size, so one chunk is one 16-byte load. Placing chunk j of every token in the block next to each other makes the warp's 16 simultaneous loads touch neighbouring addresses, which the GPU serves as a coalesced access. Token-major order would place them 256 bytes apart, one 16-byte piece per 256-byte row.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
question: You run a multi-tenant API on vLLM and worry that a user could tell whether a competitor recently sent a given prompt. What does vLLM provide for this?
options: Disable PagedAttention
Set the block size to 1
Switch the hash to xxhash
A per-request cache salt mixed into the first block's hash, so only requests with the same salt share cache
explain: A shared cache leaks information through time to first token. With `cache_salt`, blocks are only shared within a trust group. A faster non-cryptographic hash like xxhash raises collision risk, which the docs warn can leak data in multi-tenant setups.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: When authorisation is unclear: the Iowa courthouse arrests
question: In a network test, which situation is the closest analogue to the county owning the courthouse?
options: The client's web server runs an old Apache version
The client's domain points to servers owned and run by a hosting provider
The client uses strong passwords
The SOC was told the test window
explain: The hosting provider owns the servers, so the client alone cannot authorise testing them, just as the state could not authorise entry to county property.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Active scanning: host discovery and what each probe tells you
question: An ACK scan reports a port as unfiltered. What do you know?
options: The port is open
A packet with only ACK set reached the host and drew a RST, so the firewall lets traffic to that port through; whether a service listens is unknown
The port is closed
The firewall is stateful
explain: ACK scans map firewall rules. Open and closed ports both answer a lone ACK with RST, so 'unfiltered' only says the path is open.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Vulnerability scanners: matching versions to known flaws
question: What does the Equifax scanning failure teach about reading a clean vulnerability scan?
options: Scanners never work
Use a faster scanner
Only internal scans matter
A clean result only covers what the scanner could see and identify; without a complete asset and component inventory, vulnerable systems can be missed
explain: The component scan ran on the root directory and missed the Struts subdirectory, and the McAfee scan of 958 external addresses also found nothing. The House report adds that Equifax lacked a complete IT asset inventory. Coverage, not just the scanner, determines what a clean report means.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
question: Why should a finding's 'how to check' section avoid working attack steps?
options: Reports circulate widely; a safe check (compare versions, observe a configuration) confirms the issue and the fix without making the report a ready-made weapon
Clients never read that section
Attack steps are always wrong
Attack steps make the report too short
explain: The audience needs to confirm and retest, not attack. Version and configuration checks do that; a weaponised reproduction in a document that circulates creates new risk.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
question: Profiling a C service you built with -O2 -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Some flame graph boxes show `process` directly calling `convolve` although the code goes through `blur`. Which extra flag addresses this?
options: -fomit-frame-pointer
-mno-omit-leaf-frame-pointer
-fno-inline
explain: Skipping exactly one caller is the leaf pattern: the leaf (convolve) did not set up a frame, so rbp still pointed at blur's frame and the walk jumped straight to blur's caller. Keeping frame pointers in leaf functions fixes it. Inlining blur into process could also hide it, but then the code would no longer go through a real blur frame.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Publishing an update with one 8-byte store
question: You update a 48-byte record that readers find through a pointer. Which sequence is crash-consistent without a log?
options: Overwrite the record in place, then persist it with one pmem_persist call
Write a new copy elsewhere, persist it, store the 8-byte pointer to it, persist the pointer, and free the old copy safely afterwards
Store the new pointer first so readers move quickly, then write and persist the new copy
Overwrite in place using six 8-byte stores, each one followed by CLWB but with no fences
explain: Only the out-of-place copy keeps every crash state old or new. In-place overwrite can tear across 48 bytes. Publishing the pointer first can make it durable before the data. The free must also be crash-safe, or you get a leak or a double free.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: From mass phishing to help-desk calls
question: An attacker texts 300 employees 'Your parcel could not be delivered, pay 1.99 to rebook' with a link. Which term fits best?
options: Whaling
Mass smishing
Spear phishing by voice
Help-desk social engineering
explain: It is generic (mass) and arrives by SMS (smishing). Whaling targets a senior individual; spear phishing is tailored; help-desk attacks target IT staff by phone.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DKIM: a signature over headers and body
question: A forwarded message arrives with SPF fail but DKIM pass for d=corp.example, and the From is corp.example. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The message was forged
DKIM always passes after forwarding
The forwarder's IP is not in corp.example's SPF record, but the signature survived because the content was unchanged
SPF and DKIM check the same thing, so one of them is broken
explain: Forwarding changes the connecting IP, which breaks SPF, but leaves the signed headers and body intact, so DKIM still verifies. This is exactly why DKIM was needed alongside SPF.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Lookalike domains and homoglyphs
question: A filter flags only domains that mix Latin and Cyrillic letters in one label. Which lookalike of 'apple.com' slips through?
options: xn--80ak6aa92e.com (all five letters Cyrillic)
xn--pple-43d.com (Cyrillic a + Latin pple)
apple.com
None; mixed-script checks catch every homoglyph
explain: All-Cyrillic labels are single-script, so a mixed-script rule passes them. UTS 39 calls this a whole-script confusable; skeleton comparison catches it.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
question: Your company's simulated phishing click rate dropped from 12 percent to 6 percent, but reports of real phish also dropped by half. What does the NCSC's guidance suggest?
options: Celebrate; clicks halved
Make the simulations harder until clicks reach zero
Investigate: falling reports may mean people fear blame, and reporting is the early-warning signal you need
Stop all reporting to reduce noise
explain: The NCSC warns that metrics valuing the absence of problems incentivise silence, and recommends measuring how many people report. Fewer reports means slower detection of the phish that do get through.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: How the compiler lays out a struct, field by field
question: `struct S { char a; double d; char b; };` on x86-64. What are `offsetof(S, d)` and `sizeof(S)`?
options: 8 and 17
1 and 10
4 and 16
8 and 24
explain: a at 0, then padding to 8 for d (alignment 8), d fills 8 to 15, b at 16, end at 17, rounded up to a multiple of 8 gives 24.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Byte order: reading and writing multi-byte fields on the wire
question: Which way of reading a big-endian `uint32_t` at offset 3 of a received buffer is correct on both little- and big-endian hosts and at any alignment?
options: Shift and OR the four bytes, most significant first
Cast `buf + 3` to `uint32_t *` and call ntohl on the result
memcpy into a packed struct and read the field without conversion
Declare the field as a bit-field of width 32
explain: Byte reads have no alignment or byte order, so the shift-and-or decoder is correct everywhere and compiles to a load plus a byte reverse. The cast is misaligned and breaks the aliasing rule; the packed struct gets the order wrong on little-endian hosts; bit-field layout is implementation-defined.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
question: A team swaps a 64x48 heatmap head for a 16x12 one to save compute, keeping the same decoder. What do you expect on COCO AP?
options: No change, because the quarter offset fixes quantization
An increase, because coarser maps are smoother
A drop, mostly at strict thresholds, because each cell now covers 16x16 input pixels
A drop only for keypoints that are occluded
explain: Quantization error grows with cell size, and a quarter-cell shift only removes part of it. Strict OKS thresholds such as 0.75 punish a few pixels of error, so they suffer first.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: What a quantum computer breaks, and what it only dents
question: Patient records must stay confidential for 25 years. Your migration will take 5 years, and estimates for a CRQC range from 10 to 20 years. What does Mosca's inequality tell you?
options: Even at the late estimate, 25 + 5 = 30 exceeds 20, so records sent with classical key exchange today are already at risk from recorded traffic
Nothing yet: wait until the estimates narrow
Only signatures on the records need to change
Upgrade AES-128 to AES-256 first
explain: X + Y = 30 is greater than every plausible Z, so harvest-now-decrypt-later already applies. Key establishment protecting these records should move to ML-KEM (in practice a hybrid) first; AES-128 is not the weak point.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Encrypting one bit with LWE, by hand
question: In the toy (q = 41), decrypting an encryption of bit 1 gives d = 18. Why is that read as 1?
options: Because 18 is even
Because the secret s was used
Because d is never 0 for bit 1
Because 18 lies between 10 and 30, the band around q/2 = 20; the extra -2 is summed noise
explain: Decryption checks which of 0 or 20 the value is closer to (the band 10 < d < 30 means 1). The 2 missing from 20 is the sum of the errors of the chosen rows.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: SLH-DSA, LMS and XMSS: signatures from hash functions alone
question: Your firmware signer uses LMS on a virtual machine that operations staff restore from last night's snapshot after a crash. What is the risk?
options: None: LMS is stateless
The public key changes
Signatures become larger
The restored state points at one-time keys that were already used, so the next signatures reuse them and an attacker who sees both can forge signatures
explain: Rolling back state is the classic way stateful hash-based keys get reused. SP 800-208 requires signing in a hardware module that does not export keys; or use stateless SLH-DSA where that is impractical.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Deadlines and a migration plan you can defend
question: Under IR 8547, an ECDSA P-384 signing key is still in use in 2032. What is its status?
options: Disallowed: all classical signatures were disallowed after 2030
Deprecated: still usable if the data owner accepts the risk, and disallowed after 2035 under NIST standards
Acceptable, because P-384 gives 192-bit classical security
Legacy use only: it can verify but not sign
explain: IR 8547 deprecates quantum-vulnerable signatures after 2030 regardless of strength and disallows them after 2035. Federal high value assets face the earlier OMB deadlines on top of that.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity
question: An Elasticsearch shard holds a single segment, k = 10 and default num_candidates. The kNN filter matches 12 documents in that segment. What does Lucene do?
options: Walks the HNSW graph and returns at most 10 of the 12
Skips the graph and scores the 12 matching documents directly
Runs the unfiltered search, then applies the filter as a post-filter
Raises an error because matches are fewer than num_candidates
explain: Default num_candidates is 1.5 x 10 = 15. Since 12 matches is no more than 15, Lucene's documented rule skips the graph and brute-forces the 12 filtered documents for that segment.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Latency versus bandwidth: two different walls
question: Which workload is most likely latency-bound once its data is far larger than the caches?
options: Summing a large float array
Copying a 2 GB buffer with memcpy
Descending a pointer-based binary search tree with random keys
Adding two large vectors element by element
explain: Each tree level's child pointer comes from the node just loaded, so misses happen one after another. The other three compute every address from a loop index, so many lines can be requested in parallel and the limit is bytes per second.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Bandwidth-bound code: count the bytes, skip the reads
question: A single-threaded loop streams through a 4 GB array and achieves 11 GB/s on a server whose memory system delivers 150 GB/s across all cores. Adding software prefetches does not help. What is the most promising next step?
options: Switch to non-temporal stores, since it must be bandwidth-bound
Convert the array to a linked list
Split the work across several threads so more lines are in flight in total
Disable the hardware prefetcher
explain: 11 of 150 GB/s is far from peak, so this is not the bandwidth wall. A single core's concurrency (fill buffers plus L2 queues) caps it, as Little's law predicts. More cores bring more miss slots. Non-temporal stores reduce bytes, which matters only near the peak.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Sparse data: how a few ratings re-identified Netflix users
question: Why does the Netflix attack weight each movie by 1 / log(number of people who rated it)?
options: To normalise ratings between 1 and 5
Because matching on a rarely rated movie is much stronger evidence of identity than matching on a popular one
To make the algorithm faster
Because popular movies have more rating errors
explain: A match on a film rated by 40 people narrows the candidates far more than a match on one rated by 200,000. The weight turns that intuition into a score; rare items dominate.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy: a promise about one person
question: Why is randomized response ln 3-DP and not 0-DP?
options: Because the coins are not fair
Because the analyst can recover p
Because a true 'Yes' gives answer 'Yes' with probability 3/4 but a true 'No' gives it with probability 1/4, a ratio of 3
Because some people lie
explain: The answer still depends on the truth: 3/4 versus 1/4. The worst-case ratio of 3 gives epsilon = ln 3. Recovering the population rate is allowed and is the point of the mechanism.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Designing for less: data minimisation and purpose limitation
question: Why is a purpose check in application code not enough on its own?
options: Because Python is not secure
Because anyone with direct database access, or code that bypasses the access function, is not bound by it
Because purposes cannot be expressed in code
Because the GDPR forbids code checks
explain: The check binds callers that use it. Database grants that physically deny the analytics role access, plus access logs, close the bypass.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Data protection impact assessments that change the design
question: Under Article 35(7), which question belongs in a DPIA but not in a typical security review?
options: Is the data encrypted at rest?
Which CVEs affect the servers?
Is this processing necessary and proportionate to its purpose, or would less data do?
Is multi-factor authentication enabled?
explain: Necessity and proportionality ask whether the processing should happen at this scale at all. Encryption, patching and MFA are security measures that a DPIA may list, but they do not answer that question.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts
question: A systemd service runs `ExecStart=/home/dev/tools/agent` and its unit has no `User=` line. Developers can edit files in their home directories. What is the best fix?
options: Add `NoNewPrivileges=yes` to the unit
Make /home/dev/tools/agent mode 700
Move the binary to a root-owned directory and run the service as a dedicated unprivileged user
Restart the service less often
explain: Without User=, the service runs as root, so whoever controls the file controls root. Moving it to a root-owned path removes the write path, and running as its own user limits the damage even if something else goes wrong. NoNewPrivileges does not help when the process already is root.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Windows escalation 3: UAC bypass, vulnerable drivers, PrintNightmare
question: A user with a standard (non-admin) account runs a published UAC bypass. What happens?
options: They get SYSTEM
They get a high-integrity administrator token
Nothing useful: a standard user has no administrator token for the bypass to unlock
UAC is disabled for all users on the machine
explain: UAC bypasses skip the consent prompt between an administrator's filtered token and full token. A standard user has only one, unprivileged token. That is why standard accounts for daily work blunt this whole class.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Lateral movement channels and the logs each one leaves
question: On a file server you see 4624 type 3 from an admin account, then 7045 for a service called `XYZSVC` with an image path in `C:\Windows\`, then a process started by services.exe. What happened most likely?
options: Someone logged in at the console
A remote execution tool used SMB and a temporary service to run a command
A scheduled task ran
RDP session reconnected
explain: A network logon followed by a freshly installed service and a child of services.exe is the SMB-plus-service pattern (T1021.002 with T1569.002). Console logons are type 2, RDP is type 10, and scheduled tasks write their own events.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
question: You train a PRM where every token of a step (not just the separator) carries the step's label. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; more labeled tokens means more signal
The loss can no longer be cross-entropy
Separators stop being tokenized
Tokens early in a step are trained to predict the verdict of text they have not seen yet, and long steps dominate the loss
explain: A causal model at an early token has not read the rest of the step, so it would be trained to guess a label that depends on future tokens, and steps with many tokens would weigh more. Putting the label only on the separator asks for the verdict once the whole step is visible.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Using a PRM: reranking, step-level search and RL
question: Your PPO run with a summed PRM reward shows mean response length doubling while accuracy stays flat. Which fix bounds the problem?
options: Raise the PRM's learning rate so it adapts faster
Switch the reduction from product to minimum at inference
Use more rollouts per step when labeling
Reward each step with its PRM score minus the next step's (Delta), so a trajectory's total reward is bounded by one step's score
explain: Summed per-step rewards grow with the number of steps, so padding pays. Delta makes the sum telescope to the first step's score; Clip makes every step reward non-positive. Both cap the return of any trajectory (Gao et al., 2024).

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share
question: A 16 GiB database process calls `fork()` to take a snapshot, and the child only reads memory and writes it to disk while the parent keeps serving writes. Which cost grows over time?
options: None: copy-on-write means fork never copies data
The child's reads, because reading a shared page triggers a copy
The parent's writes: each first write to a still-shared page faults and copies that page, so memory use grows with the number of distinct pages the parent modifies
The initial fork, which copies all 16 GiB before returning
explain: Reads of shared pages are free. Each page the parent modifies while the child still maps it must be copied once, so both memory use and page-fault work grow with the parent's write set during the snapshot.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
question: You benchmark a context switch with a ping-pong of two processes that touch no memory, and get 2 microseconds. Your real service switches 5,000 times a second between processes with 400 KB working sets on a CPU with a 512 KB cache. What should you expect?
options: About 1 percent overhead, since 5,000 x 2 us = 10 ms per second
No overhead, since the working sets fit in cache
Noticeably more than 1 percent, because each switch also refills cache the other process evicted, and the benchmark measured none of that
Less than 1 percent, because larger working sets amortize the switch
explain: Two 400 KB working sets do not fit in a 512 KB cache together, the regime where Li et al. saw tens to hundreds of microseconds per switch. The empty ping-pong measures only the direct cost.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
question: Your ADC distances are consistently smaller than the true distances. Is that a bug?
options: Yes: ADC should be unbiased because the query is exact
Yes: you forgot the square roots
No: the paper shows the estimator underestimates on average, and ranking does not need the bias removed
No: but you must add the correction term or recall collapses
explain: Jegou et al. show d(x, q(y)) underestimates on average. Adding the expected distortion removes the bias but increases variance, and in their experiments the corrected version gave inferior search results. Correct it only if you need the distance values themselves, for example for a radius threshold.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Beyond slices: residual and additive quantizers
question: Why does an L2 index over additive codes store each vector's norm, while PQ does not need one?
options: Because additive codes are signed and PQ codes are not
Because PQ's slices are disjoint, so the squared distance splits into per-slice table entries; overlapping additive codewords leave cross terms, so Faiss uses the norm plus an inner-product table
Because the norm is needed to normalize vectors for cosine similarity
Because additive quantizers cannot compute inner products
explain: For PQ, the squared distance to a reconstruction is a sum of per-slice squared distances, each in a table. For a sum of overlapping codewords, the squared norm contains pairwise dot products between codewords. Inner products still split, so storing the squared norm of the reconstruction recovers L2 from an inner-product table.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: DSPy: signatures, modules and optimizers
question: You want to tune both the instruction and the demos of each predictor, your metric returns only a number (no textual feedback), and you have a moderate budget. Which optimizer do the DSPy docs point to?
options: LabeledFewShot
KNNFewShot
BootstrapFinetune
MIPROv2
explain: MIPROv2 searches instructions and demos jointly with Bayesian optimization and treats the metric as a black-box scalar. GEPA is the other strong option but gets most of its power from textual feedback in the metric; LabeledFewShot and KNNFewShot only choose demos; BootstrapFinetune changes weights.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: A residue is a rigid frame: rotation plus translation
question: You rotate an entire generated protein by 90 degrees about the z axis. What happens to the frames?
options: Every frame's rotation is left-multiplied by the same rotation and every translation is rotated; the protein is unchanged in substance
Only the translations change; the rotations are stored in local coordinates and are unaffected
Only the rotations change; CA positions are absolute and never move
The frames become invalid because the columns of R are no longer orthonormal
explain: A global rigid motion acts on every frame identically: each R becomes (global R) times R and each x becomes (global R) x plus the translation. The protein itself is the same object, which is exactly the symmetry an SE(3) model is built to respect.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Why security teams script, and your first Python program
question: Line 10 of count_failed.py is changed to `if "failed" in line:`. What does the script print for the same five lines?
options: failed logins: 4
failed logins: 5
An error, because in only works on lists
failed logins: 0
explain: `in` is case-sensitive. The lines contain `Failed` with a capital F, never `failed`, so nothing matches and the count is 0. Use `"failed" in line.lower()` when you want a case-insensitive check. `in` works on strings as well as lists.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Hashing files and checking them against known-bad lists
question: Your script reports "0 matches" after hashing every file on a server against 20,000 SHA-256 IOCs from a vendor feed. What can you honestly conclude?
options: The server is clean
The feed must be broken
The attacker used MD5 instead
None of the files is an exact copy of a listed file
explain: Hash matching only detects byte-identical copies. Recompiled, repacked or slightly edited malware has a different hash, and so do files the feed never saw. Report what you actually tested.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
question: Which call is safe when `domain` comes from an alert?
options: subprocess.run(f"whois {domain}", shell=True)
subprocess.run("whois " + domain, shell=True)
os.system("whois " + domain)
subprocess.run(["whois", domain], timeout=30)
explain: Only the list form avoids the shell. The two shell=True strings and os.system all pass the text to /bin/sh, where a semicolon or backtick in domain starts a new command. Validating domain against a strict pattern is still a good second layer.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Where synonym rules come from: logs, clicks and embeddings
question: In the toy click table, iphone case and iphone charger have a co-click Jaccard of 0.67, the same as laptop and notebook computer. Should `iphone case, iphone charger` become a synonym rule?
options: Yes: equal co-click scores mean equally good rules
Yes, but only as an index-time rule so it costs nothing at query time
No: they are complementary products sharing a bundle and a photo; a rule would show chargers to people looking for cases
No: Jaccard is only valid for single-word queries
explain: Co-clicks show the queries are related, not interchangeable. Jones et al. would grade it a possible rewrite (complementary product), not a precise one. Related-search suggestions are a fine use; synonym expansion is not.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: LLM expansion prompts, and deciding per query whether to expand
question: A support search sends every query through an LLM rewrite. `error E1234 on X200 printer` comes back as `Why does my printer show an error message?`. What breaks, and what guard prevents it?
options: Nothing: the rewrite is more fluent, so BM25 will rank better
BM25 cannot index digits, so the original query never worked either
It dropped E1234 and X200, the matching page's only distinctive terms; keep the original query in the expanded one and skip expansion for queries with codes or model numbers
The LLM should have expanded E1234 into synonyms such as E1235
explain: Identifiers are rare terms with high IDF and exactly what the relevant page contains. A rewrite that drops them replaces precise evidence with generic words. Repeating the original query (as query2doc does) keeps them, and a rule that skips expansion when the query contains codes avoids the risk entirely.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Decomposition: Self-Ask, least-to-most and sub-query evidence
question: Why can no single rewrite of the Orion question reliably retrieve d2 (Mira Patel earned a degree at Lakeside University)?
options: Because BM25 cannot handle long queries
Because d2 is too short
Because the words that identify d2, Mira Patel, are a bridge entity known only after the first hop
Because d2 has the same score as d4
explain: d2 is about Mira Patel, and the question never mentions Patel. Only after Q1 retrieves d1 does the name exist to put in a query. This is why multi-hop retrieval needs sequential decomposition, not a better single query.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Binary search plus rescoring: oversample, then re-rank
question: Why does binary quantization pair so naturally with rescoring, compared with int8 scalar quantization?
options: Binary distances are coarse with many ties, so a cheap wide first pass plus a precise second pass recovers most quality
Binary codes cannot be stored in RAM without rescoring
Rescoring is impossible with int8 vectors
Binary distances are biased upward, and rescoring subtracts the bias
explain: 1 bit per dimension loses a lot of ranking detail, so the first stage is best used as a filter. Rescoring works with int8 too (Hugging Face shows it), it just matters less there.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ inside an index: IVF clusters, graphs and fast rotations
question: With nprobe = 8, why does IVF-RaBitQ not multiply the query by P^-1 eight times?
options: Each cluster uses its own random rotation
P^-1 is linear: P^-1 (q_r - c_k) = P^-1 q_r - P^-1 c_k, and P^-1 c_k is stored at index time
The query is not normalized in IVF-RaBitQ
Only the first probed cluster needs a rotated query
explain: One rotation of the raw query plus one stored rotated centroid per cluster gives every re-centered query by subtraction; dividing by the already known centroid distance normalizes it. All clusters share one rotation P.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Business logic flaws: when correct code does the wrong thing
question: Which of these is a business logic flaw rather than an injection or configuration bug?
options: A search box passes its input into an SQL query, so a quote character causes a database error
A shop grants a threshold discount when the code is entered and keeps it after items are removed
A server still accepts TLS 1.0 connections
A comment field renders HTML tags from other users
explain: The discount bug breaks no technical rule: each request is valid and the code does what it was told. The rule (discount only while the cart is 1000 or more) was checked at the wrong time. The others are injection, protocol configuration and cross-site scripting.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
question: In the lost-update variant, five withdrawals of 100 succeed and the final balance reads 0. Why is this worse than ending at -400?
options: The balance looks valid, so nothing flags the 400 paid out without funds until payouts are reconciled
It is not worse, both lose the same amount
Because 0 cannot be stored in the database
Because the user can withdraw again
explain: With -400, an obvious invariant (balance never negative) is visibly broken. With 0, the account looks normal and the loss hides in the difference between recorded payouts and the balance, which only reconciliation finds.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
question: An app uses SERIALIZABLE isolation and logs SQLSTATE 40001 errors but returns them to users as "transfer failed". What is missing?
options: Nothing, a failed transfer is the safe outcome
A switch back to Read Committed
A retry of the whole transaction from the beginning, as PostgreSQL's documentation requires
A FOR UPDATE on every SELECT
explain: Serialization failures are expected under SERIALIZABLE; the database aborted one transaction to keep the result consistent. Retrying the whole transaction gives honest users their transfer (and a racing duplicate a correct refusal). Returning the error is safe but makes ordinary concurrent use fail.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Detecting and responding to logic and race abuse
question: A wallet balance reads 0 and no alert fired, but its ledger sums to -400. Which detection caught the problem, and what kind of race left it?
options: A burst rule; a limit overrun with a negative balance
A web application firewall (WAF) signature; SQL injection
Reconciliation of balance against ledger; a lost update, where later writes overwrote earlier ones
A rate limit; credential stuffing
explain: The balance itself looks valid, so only comparing it with the ledger reveals the gap. A lost update (writing a value computed from a stale read) produces exactly this: five recorded payouts, one visible debit.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
question: A follower's log has entries with terms [1, 1, 2] at indexes 1 to 3. It receives AppendEntries with prevLogIndex = 3, prevLogTerm = 3 and one new entry. What happens?
options: It appends the entry at index 4
It overwrites entry 3 with term 3 and appends
It rejects; the leader will retry with a smaller nextIndex
It starts an election because the leader looks stale
explain: The follower's entry 3 has term 2, not 3, so the consistency check fails and it refuses the request. The leader decrements nextIndex and retries until it finds the last index where both logs agree; only then are conflicting entries replaced.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Indexing: how chunk size and overlap decide what can be found
question: Why did overlap 4 make the People team fact retrievable as one chunk in D1?
options: Overlap makes the embedding model weight the last words of a chunk higher
Overlap removes stopwords at chunk boundaries
Overlap guarantees every sentence is whole in exactly one chunk
With windows starting every 8 words, S6 (words 34 to 44) fits wholly inside the window covering words 32 to 44
explain: Overlap does not guarantee anything about sentences; it only shifts where windows start. Here the shifted window D1.5 happens to contain all of S6. A sentence longer than the stride can still be cut in every window, which is why structure-aware splitters exist.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: The seven failure points and how to debug them
question: Logs show the correct chunk at rank 2 from the retriever, but it never appears in the final prompt because the prompt builder deduplicates by document and keeps only the first chunk per document. Which failure point is this?
options: FP 2 Missed the Top Ranked Documents
FP 3 Not in Context
FP 4 Not Extracted
FP 1 Missing Content
explain: Retrieval succeeded: the chunk ranked 2nd. It was lost during consolidation into the context, which is FP 3. Raising k would not help; the consolidation rule has to change.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Normalization and missing values
question: You fit min-max normalization on last month's training data (views max 95000). Today a document has 400000 views. What does the serving-time normalizer produce, and is that a problem?
options: Exactly 1.0, nothing to worry about
An error, because the value is out of range
0, because unknown values default to zero
About 4.2, outside the range the model was trained on
explain: Min-max uses the stored constants: (400000 - 12) / (95000 - 12) is about 4.2. A linear model extrapolates past anything it saw; a tree treats it like the largest training value. Clipping, log transforms or rank-based encodings make this less surprising.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: nDCG precisely: gain, discount, log base and the ideal
question: You switch your nDCG@10 code from log2 to natural log in the discount, keeping everything else fixed. What happens to the scores?
options: Every nDCG@10 changes by the factor ln 2
Nothing: the constant factor cancels between DCG and ideal DCG
Ranks 1 and 2 become undiscounted
nDCG can now exceed 1
explain: log_e(i+1) = ln 2 times log2(i+1) for every rank, so both the run's DCG and the ideal DCG are scaled by the same factor 1/ln 2, which cancels. Raw DCG does change, and so does the original Jarvelin-Kekalainen form, where the base also decides how many ranks escape discounting.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: A crime with a supply chain: the roles and the money
question: Why did LockBit advertise that its affiliates receive the ransom first and then send the core its cut?
options: It reduced the affiliate's risk of being cheated by the core, which helped recruit affiliates
It let LockBit avoid sanctions because the core never touched the money
It was required by the cryptocurrency exchanges the group used
It made the payment untraceable for law enforcement
explain: CISA lists it among LockBit's ways to attract affiliates, in contrast to groups that pay themselves first. Affiliates carry the risk of the intrusion and fear not being paid; who holds the money first decides who can cheat whom. It does not affect sanctions or traceability.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Inside: from one login to Domain Admin to the hypervisor
question: Why did CVE-2024-37085 let any domain user who could create groups become an ESXi administrator?
options: ESXi stored the root password in AD
Domain users are local admins on ESXi by default
ESXi trusted a group by its name, so a newly created group called ESX Admins was given full admin rights
The group's SID was hard-coded in ESXi
explain: Microsoft found that domain-joined ESXi granted full admin to members of a group named ESX Admins, without checking that the group existed beforehand and matching it by name, not SID. Creating the group with that name was enough.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Hardening that actually blocks the path
question: An organisation enforces MFA on its VPN, but its ESXi hosts take admin rights from AD. An attacker phishes a help desk into resetting an employee's MFA and later becomes domain admin. Which control from the matrix would still stop mass VM encryption?
options: Phishing-resistant MFA on the VPN
Egress baselining
Approved RMM only
ESXi admin authentication separated from AD, with lockdown mode
explain: Once AD is owned, any system that trusts AD for admin rights falls with it. ESXi hosts with local, per-host credentials and lockdown mode do not. The other controls address earlier steps the attacker already passed.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Why sockets cost microseconds and cores, and what RDMA removes
question: You already use `sendfile` so the server never copies file bytes into user space. Which cost does RDMA remove that `sendfile` still pays?
options: Running the transport protocol and a system call on the host CPU for each message
The copy from the page cache into a socket buffer
The DMA from host memory to the NIC
The need to know the destination address
explain: `sendfile` already avoids the user-space copy, and DMA between memory and the NIC happens in both designs. What stays with sockets is the kernel: a system call per operation and the TCP stack running on a CPU per packet. RDMA moves the transport into the NIC and lets the application post work without entering the kernel.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Two-sided SEND versus one-sided READ, WRITE and atomics
question: You want one server to accept requests from 10,000 clients with as little NIC state as possible. Which transport fits, and what does it give up?
options: UD: one QP can talk to every client, but only SEND/RECV of at most one MTU per message
RC: it supports every verb
UC: it is unreliable, so it needs no state
UD: it supports RDMA READ without connections
explain: A connected QP (RC or UC) talks to exactly one peer, so 10,000 clients need 10,000 QPs. A UD QP can exchange datagrams with any UD QP, which is why designs like HERD use it for responses. The price: no RDMA READ/WRITE or atomics, no reliability, and single-MTU messages.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
question: A server receives a client frame whose MASK bit is 0. What does RFC 6455 require?
options: Close the connection, optionally with close code 1002 (protocol error)
Unmask it with a zero key and process it normally
Reply with a ping to ask the client to resend it masked
Accept it only if the connection is over TLS
explain: Section 5.1: the server MUST close the connection on an unmasked client frame and MAY send close code 1002. Masking is required whether or not TLS is used, so TLS does not make it optional.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
question: Your game streams 20 snapshots per second over WebSocket at 150 ms RTT on a lossy mobile link. Players see enemies freeze then jump. Which change addresses the root cause?
options: Enable TCP_NODELAY on the server
Move snapshots to an unreliable channel such as WebTransport datagrams, keeping reliable messages on a stream
Lower the patch rate to 5 per second
Switch from t.float32() to t.number()
explain: The freeze-then-burst pattern is head-of-line blocking: a lost packet holds back later snapshots until retransmission. TCP_NODELAY only disables Nagle batching. An unreliable channel lets newer snapshots through, and the interpolation buffer skips the gap.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
question: A two-tower model trained with plain in-batch softmax rarely retrieves the top-100 hit items, even for users who like them. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hit items appear in many batches, so they are used as negatives far more often and get pushed down; apply the logQ correction
The temperature is too high, so all scores are equal
Hit items have too few training examples
Normalizing embeddings removes popularity information
explain: In-batch negatives follow the traffic distribution, which is power-law: a few hits take most of the traffic. Yi et al. note popular items are overly penalized as negatives and subtract log p_j from each logit to correct the bias.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Rectifying the plane: card corners to millimeters
question: A colleague fits H from the card corners, but lists the mm points in the order TL, BL, BR, TR while the pixel points are TL, TR, BR, BL. What happens?
options: H maps the card onto a transposed card, so lengths along the card's width and height are swapped and measurements are wrong
OpenCV automatically sorts the points, so nothing changes
The fit fails with an error because the points are not in clockwise order
Only the sign of the result flips
explain: The solver trusts the pairing you give it. Swapped pairs still define a valid homography, just to a wrong rectangle (85.6 placed along the 53.98 side), so it returns confidently wrong numbers. This is why ArUco returns corners in a fixed order.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
question: For parallel aggregation, two workers compute partial results for group a. Worker 1 saw 30; worker 2 saw 50 and 40. What should the final step combine to get avg = 40?
options: The two averages, 30 and 45, averaged to 37.5
The two states (1, 30) and (2, 90), added to (3, 120), then 120 / 3
Only the larger worker's average, 45
The two averages weighted equally, then rounded
explain: Averaging averages gives 37.5, which is wrong. The correct merge combines transition states: counts add and sums add, then the final function divides once. PostgreSQL supports this with combine functions for partial aggregation; the merge works on states, not on finished results.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Latency: you wait for the slowest replica you need
question: N = 5, replica delays independent with the same distribution. Which choice gives the lowest 99.9th percentile write latency while still overlapping reads done with R = 3?
explain: Overlap needs $R + W > 5$, so with R = 3 the smallest valid W is 3. Latency only grows with W (you wait for a later order statistic), so W = 3 is the fastest correct choice. W = 1 or 2 is faster but breaks the overlap.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: A precise test: when is a proxy unhackable?
question: Same house, true reward [1, 1, 1]. A new proxy over-weights the attic: [3, 1, 1]. Using the 8 deterministic policies, is it hackable?
options: No: it gives positive weight to every room, so it agrees with the true reward
Yes: A alone gets proxy 3 but true 1, while B+K gets proxy 2 but true 2
No: over-weighting one room only changes ties, never strict orderings
Yes, but only for stochastic policies
explain: The proxy prefers A (3 over 2) while the true reward prefers B+K (2 over 1): a strict reversal. Positive weights on every room are not enough. A milder proxy [2, 1, 1] would tie A with B+K (2 and 2) and, by exhaustive check, has no strict reversal.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: Fixing the reward, not just the leash: ensembles, WARM, ODIN, PAR
question: You can train five reward models but afford only one reward-model forward pass per sample during RL. Which method fits?
options: A prediction ensemble with worst-case combination
A prediction ensemble with UWO
Train five RMs from scratch with different random seeds and average their weights
WARM: fine-tune five RMs from the same SFT model and average their weights
explain: Both prediction ensembles need five forward passes per sample. Weight averaging gives one model, but only works when the members share pretraining (linear mode connectivity); RMs trained from scratch do not stay connected, so their average is a broken model.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Governance, risk and compliance: three jobs and who decides
question: A developer finds that the production admin console has no multi-factor login. Under the Three Lines Model, who should decide whether to accept or fix this risk?
options: The developer, because they found it
Internal audit, because it is independent
The risk owner of the system, within their delegated authority, advised by the CISO's team
The external auditor at the next audit
explain: First-line owners own and decide on their risks, with second-line advice and challenge. Internal audit stays independent precisely so it can later judge that decision; external auditors only report.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Treating risk: accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid
question: After mitigation the residual ALE is USD 256,000 and the board's appetite allows that. What should happen next?
options: Nothing; the risk is closed
The residual risk must be transferred to insurance
The risk owner formally accepts the residual risk, recorded in the register with a review date
Mitigate until residual risk is zero
explain: Residual risk is never zero. It is accepted explicitly by someone with the authority to do so, and reviewed on a schedule.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: SOC 2: trust services criteria, Type I vs II, and your evidence
question: A vendor offers a SOC 2 Type I report dated 14 months ago. What does it tell you?
options: That its controls were suitably designed and in place on one date 14 months ago, and nothing about whether they operated since
That its controls worked for the last 14 months
That it is ISO 27001 certified
That it passed a PCI assessment
explain: Type I is a point-in-time design opinion. For operating effectiveness you need a Type II covering a recent period, plus a bridge letter for the gap since the period ended.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: EU law for engineers: GDPR, NIS2, DORA and the Cyber Resilience Act
question: Which NIS2 article makes management bodies approve and oversee cybersecurity risk-management measures and allows them to be held liable?
options: Article 20
Article 23
Article 21
Article 34
explain: Article 20 covers governance: approval, oversight, liability and mandatory training for management. Article 21 lists the measures, 23 the reporting, 34 the fines.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Cyber insurance: what it pays, what it asks, what it excludes
question: With a USD 250,000 deductible and a USD 3 million limit, how much does the company bear in a year with a USD 2 million loss?
options: USD 0
explain: The company pays the first 250,000; the insurer pays the remaining 1.75 million, which is within the limit.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: The long tail: why one response can idle a whole cluster
question: A colleague proposes doubling the number of rollout engines, each still decoding a share of one synchronous batch, to fix 51% engine idleness. What is the main flaw?
options: More engines need more weight-sync bandwidth, which is the real bottleneck
Doubling engines doubles the length of every response
Engines cannot run in parallel on one batch
The idle time is set by the longest response, and one response cannot be split across engines, so the phase still lasts as long as that response
explain: Autoregressive decoding of one response is sequential. Adding engines shortens the time to finish the short responses, but the phase still waits for the longest one, so idleness goes up. verl's fully async docs make the same point: in the colocated case, adding rollout resources cannot remove long-tail idleness.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
question: NeMo RL async GRPO runs with max_trajectory_age_steps: 1. A trajectory was generated with weights v10. At which training steps can it be used?
options: Steps 10 and 11; at step 12 it is discarded
Only step 10
Steps 9, 10 and 11
Any step, as long as importance sampling correction is on
explain: The docs' own example: a trajectory generated with v10 can be used for training steps v10 or v11, and at step v12 it is too old and is discarded. Importance correction handles the remaining mismatch; it does not remove the age limit.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Multi-turn agentic rollouts: tools, servers and token-in, token-out
question: In the toy model, tool waits grow from 1 to 20 s to 10 to 60 s. Which change keeps the inference GPUs busiest?
options: Batch per turn with a larger batch
A tighter maximum response length
Move tools onto the GPU servers
Run many more concurrent trajectories as independent coroutines, so some are always decoding while others wait on tools
explain: With independent loops, GPU idleness comes only from too few trajectories being ready to decode. More concurrent trajectories fill the gaps, which is what Kimi K2 does with a large number of concurrent rollouts; batch per turn keeps a global idle phase for every tool round.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: The four golden signals, read as distributions
question: Which single measurement best distinguishes the hypothesis that catalog is itself saturated from the hypothesis that catalog's database got slow?
options: Catalog's p99 latency, which is 1000 ms either way
Catalog's error rate of 7.41 percent
The number of catalog pods firing alerts
Catalog's pool wait time against its database query time: 988 ms waiting for a connection versus 12 ms executing the query
explain: p99, error rate and alert count are identical under both hypotheses, so none of them discriminates. Splitting the latency into time spent waiting for a resource and time spent doing work does: the query still takes 12 ms, so the database is fine and the backlog is in front of the pool. Instrument the wait and the work separately, or you cannot tell these apart during an incident.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
question: Your organisation writes excellent postmortems and the same class of incident keeps recurring. Which measurement would tell you where the process is leaking?
options: Mean time to resolution for the recurring class
Number of postmortems written per quarter
The fraction of action items with an owner, a bug and a priority that were completed, broken down by type
Number of alerts fired per incident
explain: Writing the document is not the mechanism that reduces recurrence; completing the typed, owned, tracked items is. Counting postmortems measures effort, and MTTR measures response rather than prevention. If completion is low, the leak is in prioritisation; if completion is high and recurrence continues, the items are not naming the right conditions.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: Fuse, tune and test RRF on real SciFact runs
question: Tuning per-list RRF constants on train gave +0.012 nDCG@10 over RRF(60) (p = 0.02). On the held-out test claims the tuned setting is 0.002 lower (p = 0.79). Ship it?
options: Yes: the train gain was significant, and train has more queries than test
Yes, but only after re-tuning the constants on the test claims
No: switch to k = 500, since large k is safest
No: the gain did not transfer to held-out queries, so keep k = 60 (or test a score fusion, which held up in this run)
explain: A train-split gain is only a hypothesis; the held-out test is the check, and it found nothing. Re-tuning on test leaks the test set into the choice. k = 500 is not safer, just another untested choice. In this SciFact run, min-max CombSUM and CombMNZ beat RRF(60) on both train and test, so a score fusion is the better thing to test next.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
question: In C, a driver function takes a spinlock, calls a helper that returns an error, and returns early without unlocking. Which part of the Rust version prevents the equivalent bug?
options: The borrow checker forbids early returns while a lock is held
lockdep runs at compile time in Rust
The guard returned by `lock()` is dropped on every exit path, and its `Drop` calls the backend's unlock
Rust spinlocks are released automatically by the scheduler
explain: Early returns are allowed; they simply run destructors for live locals. `Guard::drop` calls `B::unlock`. lockdep still runs at runtime as in C; the Guard constructor even asserts the lock is held.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
question: The sample's ioctl returns `Err(ENOTTY)` for an unknown command. What does the userspace `ioctl()` call return?
options: 0, because the Rust error is swallowed by the trampoline
-25 directly as the return value
-1, with errno set to 25 (ENOTTY)
The process receives SIGSEGV
explain: `ENOTTY` is 25. The trampoline returns `err.to_errno()` = -25 to the VFS (virtual file system, the layer that dispatched the call to the driver). The system call returns -25 to the C library, which stores 25 in `errno` and returns -1. The userspace test in the sample prints this with `perror`.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
question: Two CPU-bound tasks at the same nice share one CPU under EEVDF. X requests a 0.5 ms slice, Y requests 4 ms. What share does X get in the long run?
options: About 89 percent, since 4 / (4 + 0.5) of the deadlines favor X
About 11 percent, since X asks for so little each time
About 50 percent: equal weights, X just runs in shorter, more frequent pieces
It depends on HZ, because slices end on ticks
explain: Share follows weight. Eligibility ($v_i \le V$) stops X from running ahead of the average however early its deadlines are. The short request only makes X run sooner and in smaller pieces.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
question: Your loader opened and loaded the skeleton without errors, but /sys/kernel/sched_ext/state still says disabled. Which step is missing?
options: The verifier has not run yet
Creating DSQ 0
Attaching the struct_ops map (SCX_OPS_ATTACH, bpf_map__attach_struct_ops)
